newsitem.title: USA: GOLF-AUGUSTA NATIONAL'S 15TH POSES BIGGER THREAT.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-AUGUSTA NATIONAL'S 15TH POSES BIGGER THREAT.

text.p: A subtle but intriguing change has been made to one of Augusta National's most storied -- and pivotal -- holes for this year's Masters, and Bobby Jones would be pleased.

The left front green on the par-five 15th hole -- where Gene Sarazen hit his "shot heard 'round the world" in 1935, a holed four-wood -- has been slightly flattened, offering a new and potentially dangerous pin placement on the 500-yard hole, which has played a crucial role in many Masters.

Tournament officials will now be able to cut the hole tantalizing close to the pond that fronts the wide green on the relatively short hole, where players are often tempted to go for the green on their second shots.

That is the exact philosphy that Jones, one of the greatest golfers ever, espoused as he oversaw the development of the Masters and Augusta National, the only permanent home for any of golf's four major championships -- but also a private club.

"Obviously, with a course wide open as needed to accomodate the average golfer, we can only tighten it up by increasing the difficulty around the greens," Jones explained in his 1959 book "Golf Is My Game."
"This we attempt to do during the tournament by placing the flags in more difficult and exacting positions and by increasing the speed of the greens."

Any golfer who has played the historic 6,925-yard, par-72 course, which was designed by the great Scotish architect Alister Mackenzie in consultation with Jones, will swear that the huge, undulating greens cannot be made any faster.
That leaves pin placement as one of the few weapons the protectors of Augusta's vaulted reputation have against today's professionals and their high-tech equipment.
But Jones -- who played with hickory shafts when he became the last player to win golf's Grand Slam in 1930 -- knew that advances in equipment would be a constant threat to the game.

"I believe that it is true that with modern equipment and with modern players, we cannot make the golf course more difficult or more testing for the expert simply by adding length," Jones wrote. "The only way to stir them up is by adding subtleties around the greens."

The change to the 15th green this year is subtle, but just enough to allow a "fair" hole placement in an area where the pond comes most into play -- and far away from the traditional "bail out" area to the right side.
With the new pin placement now available in the front left of the wide green, more splash shots can be expected this year.

The 15th -- Augusta's last real birdie opportunity -- has played a key role in many Masters in the six decades since Sarazen used his double eagle, or albatross, to gain a playoff, which he won the next day.

In 1986 Jack Nicklaus eagled the 15th in the final round on his way to his record sixth green jacket while Seve Ballesteros, his closest competitor, hit the water for a bogey and finished two shots adrift.
A year earlier Curtis Strange, leading by two on Sunday, also found the pond and finished two strokes behind Bernhard Langer of Germany.
The 15th also played a part in Langer's second victory, in 1993, when he was battling Chip Beck head-on in the final twosome on the last day.

Beck was roundly, but not universally, criticised for not trying to reach the green with his second shot when he was trailing by three with holes running out. Beck managed a par but Langer birdied to clinch the title.

The next year Jose Maria Olazabal, battling Tom Lehman down the stretch, hit a five-iron second that barely hung on the top of the bank. Taking advantage of the lucky break, he rolled in the 30-foot eagle putt. Lehman had an even shorter eagle putt but it just missed and the Spaniard won his first major.
The 15th even had a role in last year's memorable final round, according to Greg Norman.
By the time Norman and Nick Faldo reached the 15th on Sunday the Australian had squandered a six-stroke lead and Faldo, the 1989 and 1990 champion, was ahead by two.
"Until that point I still thought I could win the tournament," Norman told GOLF Magazine.
"I was just off the front of the green, lying two with a makable pitch shot for eagle.

"I put every ounce of my concentration and energy into that shot -- mental, physical, visual -- every bit of control I had in my system ... I was sure the shot was going to drop, and when it didn't my whole body was just gone. Mentally and physically, I was just gone."
Norman succumbed to a 78 while Faldo shot 67, the best round of the day, to win by five shots.
While the 15th hole ranked the hardest of Augusta's four par-fives last year, the field still played it in an average 4.88 strokes, which did not surprise Sarazen, now 94.
"It's always been an easy par five," The Squire likes to say. "But it's still a hard double eagle."
